name: The Manchester Poplar

location.address: Annie Lees Playing Fields, Mount Road, Gorton, Manchester M18 7BQ

access: Free, in a public park (Annie Lees Playing Fields), open during daylight hours
transport: Gorton railway station, about a 20 minute walk
verify_notes: Native black poplar (Populus nigra subsp. betulifolia), the UK's most endangered native tree and the species the city is informally named after ('Manchester Poplar'). Girth ~4.07m (13ft) per Woodland Trust, cited identically by both sources. Age is explicitly undocumented in both sources ('nobody knows its exact age' / 'age is a complete enigma'); both call it clearly very old given its size, so leave age_estimate empty per the honesty rule rather than guess from girth (no published growth-rate source found for this subspecies in this pass). Survived Manchester's industrial-era soot and acid rain that killed most trees in the city centre, which is exactly why black poplars are nicknamed 'Manchester poplars' locally. Shortlisted for the Woodland Trust's UK Tree of the Year 2023 (national shortlist, lost to another entry per later news, not confirmed either way this pass). Protected by a Tree Preservation Order per elmhousetreeservices.co.uk. Location: park-level coordinate only (Nominatim centroid of Annie Lees Playing Fields); no OSM natural=tree node found for the individual tree via Overpass (empty result in the park bounding box), so location_precision is approximate, not confirmed. A second, younger poplar of the same species/nickname is planted in St John's Gardens in the city centre (Castlefield, former churchyard redeveloped as a garden in 1932) -- do not conflate the two; this entry is specifically the older Gorton specimen, which is the one both sources treat as the remarkable/oldest one.

name: Adam's Laburnum

location.address: Fletcher Moss Botanical Garden / Parsonage Gardens, Stenner Lane, Didsbury, Manchester M20 2RQ

access: Free, in a public park/botanical garden. Didsbury Civic Society places the specimen in Parsonage Gardens, the walled garden by the Old Parsonage on Stenner Lane, which adjoins and is reached through Fletcher Moss Botanical Garden; look among the 'several magnificent old trees' in front of the Old Parsonage house.
transport: East Didsbury railway station, about a 10 minute walk (per Fletcher Moss Botanical Garden's own Wikipedia entry); East Didsbury Metrolink stop, about a 15 minute walk
verify_notes: A graft-chimaera, not a true species: in 1825 the Parisian nurseryman Jean Louis Adam grafted a purple broom (Chamaecytisus purpureus) onto common laburnum (Laburnum anagyroides) rootstock, and the graft union itself started sprouting a genetic mosaic of both parents, producing a small tree that is genuinely one plant with two identities: some branches flower laburnum-yellow, some broom-purple, some an intermediate dull pink. It is consequently a horticultural rarity almost everywhere it grows, and this specimen is named by the council's RHS-funded survey (Dr Owen Johnson) as 'a designated champion tree in The Tree Register for the British Isles (TROBI)', which is the recognised champion-tree registry for Britain and Ireland (the direct TROBI database is membership-only and could not be queried this pass to confirm the exact TROBI record). Didsbury Civic Society independently confirms the tree's presence and survival ('a very rare specimen of an early bio-engineered tree, that still survives today', page last updated 2020-12-06). No planting date or age found for this individual specimen; the species itself is a known 19th-century origin but that says nothing about when this particular tree was planted at Fletcher Moss/Parsonage Gardens, so age_estimate is left empty rather than bridging the two facts. Qualifies on rarity and historical/horticultural significance, not on age: the story should not imply this is an old tree, only a genuinely unusual and internationally rare one, still alive today.
